```{r, include = FALSE}
# rasters kept in the source repository (inst/extdata) but not shipped in the
# built package: read from the repository, or from GitHub when run elsewhere
load_raster_repo <- function(name) {
  paths <- file.path(c("inst/extdata", "../inst/extdata", "../../inst/extdata"), name)
  local <- paths[file.exists(paths)][1]
  if (!is.na(local)) return(terra::rast(local))
  terra::rast(paste0("/vsicurl/https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Qonfluens/spacemodR/main/inst/extdata/", name))
}
```

# Introduction

In this vignette, we explore the database linking OCS-GE
(French GIS layer for Occupation du Sol à Grande Échelle) 
labels with species labels.

We will analyze how different land cover types act as habitats with
varying qualities or resistances for different species,
starting with the Wood mouse (Apodemus sylvaticus).

```{r setup}
library(spacemodR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(terra)
library(tidyterra)
library(sf)
library(leaflet)
library(patchwork)
```

# The database construction


To build the habitat database for spacemod, we transitioned from traditional static mapping to a dynamic semantic analysis. Here is a breakdown of how this new methodology compares to previous standards.

## The Original Framework (O'Connor et al., 2024 ; @oconnor2024habitat)

The foundational method described by O'Connor et al. (2024) relies on an "expert-based" crosswalk to define optimal habitats for European terrestrial vertebrates. It links a European land systems map—which accounts for both land cover and land use intensity—to standardized habitat classifications from GlobCover and the IUCN Red List. This approach assigns simple, discrete suitability scores: 2 for optimal habitat, 1 for secondary habitat, and 0 for unsuitable. These scores were then manually penalized by subtracting points if specific keywords related to land use intensity or threats (e.g., agricultural intensification) appeared in the species' IUCN descriptions. Ultimately, this generated Area of Habitat (AOH) maps, filtering existing occurrence maps to show simple presence or absence at a 1 km² resolution.  

## The LLM-Assisted Approach for spacemod

Our approach steps away from rigid keyword matching and discrete scoring, moving toward a semantic analysis of a species' ecological requirements.Instead of using the broad European land systems, this database utilizes the fine-scale French OCS-GE (Occupation du Sol à Grande Échelle) nomenclature. Each OCS-GE code was enriched with precise ecological context. For example, paved roads are described as creating a "barrier effect," while mineral soils are noted as "thermophilic."Using a Large Language Model (Claude Opus), we fed the AI free-text descriptions of both preferred and avoided habitats (sourced from EEA databases). The model conceptually analyzed these texts against our enriched OCS-GE descriptions, with an anchored scale: 0 unused or avoided, 2 marginal, 5 secondary, 8 main, 10 core habitat.

Instead of a single presence/absence score, the model generates continuous variables (on a scale of 0 to 10) that capture finer landscape ecology concepts:

* `suitability`: Overall habitat suitability (closest to the traditional AOH score).
* `weight_breeding`: Value of the class as a breeding, nesting, denning or larval site.
* `weight_foraging`: Habitat attractiveness specifically for feeding and resource acquisition.
* `permeability`: Landscape permeability for species dispersion, which accounts for flight, swimming or fossorial habits.
* `resistance`: The impedance or barrier effect of the environment. It is derived from `permeability` on a logarithmic scale, `10^(2 * (1 - permeability / 10))`: 1 for free movement, 10 for a permeability of 5, 100 for an impassable class.

The dictionary has one row per species and OCS-GE cover (`code_us` is `NA`), and
further rows for the (cover, use) pairs where the land use changes what the cover
stands for. This vignette uses the cover alone; the article
[Habitat data sources](core_Habitat_Sources.html) shows what the land use and
other land cover maps add. The dictionary covers 935 European species, of which
482 occur in metropolitan France (column `in_france`).

## The Fundamental Difference

This new method represents a major shift in both scale and functionality. The original methodology relied on rigid keyword penalties to output a discrete matrix (0, 1, or 2), answering a simple question: can the species live in this pixel? By leveraging natural language understanding, our method generates a continuous matrix (0-10) that distinguishes between an environment where a species simply survives, one it actively seeks for food, and one it merely uses for transit. These variables are specifically designed to be injected into complex spatial ecological models (such as graph theory or Circuitscape), offering a much more nuanced view of landscape connectivity than traditional AOH mapping.

# Defining Habitat

## Weighted species habitat with OCS-GE layer for *Apodemus sylvaticus*

First, we load the necessary datasets provided by spacemodR:

1. The species dictionary assigning weights to land cover codes.
2. The OCS-GE nomenclature reference (containing names and specific hex colors).
3. The spatial layer for OCS-GE (here, we use the ocsge_metaleurop dataset as our base map).


```{r load_data}
# Load the species dict and reference tables
data("ocsge_species_dict")
data("ref_ocsge")

# Load spatial data
data("ocsge_metaleurop") 
sf_ocsge <- ocsge_metaleurop
```

We filter our species dictionary for *Apodemus sylvaticus* and join it with the 
reference nomenclature to link the OCS-GE codes to their descriptive labels and predefined colors.


```{r clean_data}
# Filter for Apodemus sylvaticus, keeping the rows of the cover alone
dfhab_Apsy <- ocsge_species_dict %>%
  filter(species_name == "Apodemus_sylvaticus", is.na(code_us))

# Join ref_ocsge with the species dictionary on the cover code
df_merged_Apsy <- ref_ocsge %>%
  dplyr::left_join(dfhab_Apsy, by = "code_cs")

# Join with the spatial sf object. Assuming sf_ocsge uses 'code_cs' (without spaces)
sf_Apsy <- sf_ocsge %>%
  dplyr::left_join(df_merged_Apsy, by = "code_cs")
```

### Understanding Habitat Values

By examining the `suitability` (s), we can classify the landscape into 
different habitat qualities for the species:

- Non-habitat area (s = 0):

```{r ex_nonhabitat}
df_merged_Apsy %>% 
  filter(suitability == 0) %>%
  pull(nomenclature) %>%
  unique()
```

- Very Poor habitat (0 < s <= 3):
```{r ex_verypoorhabitat}
df_merged_Apsy %>% 
  filter(suitability > 0, suitability <= 3) %>% 
  pull(nomenclature) %>% 
  unique()
```

- Poor habitat (3 < s <= 7):

```{r ex_poorhabitat}
df_merged_Apsy %>% 
  filter(suitability > 3, suitability <= 7) %>% 
  pull(nomenclature) %>% 
  unique()
```

- Good habitat (s > 7):

```{r ex_goodhabitat}
df_merged_Apsy %>% 
  filter(suitability > 7) %>% 
  pull(nomenclature) %>% 
  unique()
```

### Static Mapping

We will now visualize the spatial distribution of these metrics. 
We produce four maps focusing on Suitability, Foraging Weight, 
Landscape Resistance, and finally the standard OCS-GE Land Cover.

```{r mouse_staticmap, echo=FALSE}
# 4. Map: OCS-GE Nomenclature with official colors
# Create a named vector for the manual color scale
ocsge_colors <- setNames(ref_ocsge$couleur, ref_ocsge$nomenclature)
p0 <- ggplot(sf_Apsy) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = nomenclature), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = ocsge_colors, name = "OCS-GE") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Land Cover (OCS-GE Nomenclature)")


# 1. Map: Suitability
p1 <- ggplot(sf_Apsy) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = suitability), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#ffffe5", high = "#004529", na.value = "transparent", name = "Suitability") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Apodemus sylvaticus - Habitat Suitability")

# 2. Map: Foraging Weight
p2 <- ggplot(sf_Apsy) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = weight_foraging), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7fbff", high = "#08306b", na.value = "transparent", name = "Foraging\nWeight") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Apodemus sylvaticus - Foraging Weight")

# 3. Map: Resistance
p3 <- ggplot(sf_Apsy) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resistance), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#fff5f0", high = "#67000d", transform = "log10", na.value = "transparent", name = "Resistance") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Apodemus sylvaticus - Movement Resistance")

# Print maps
p0
p1
p2
p3
```

### Interactive Synthesis

To better explore the local variations and overlay different habitat
parameters for *Apodemus sylvaticus*, we combine them into a single
interactive leaflet map. You can toggle the layers in the top right corner.

```{r leaflet-apsy, fig.width=9, fig.height=6, echo=FALSE, cache=TRUE}
# Transform to WGS84 for Leaflet compatibility
sf_Apsy_wgs84 <- st_transform(sf_Apsy, 4326)

# Define color palettes
pal_wg <- colorNumeric("YlGn", domain = sf_Apsy_wgs84$suitability, na.color = "transparent")
pal_wf <- colorNumeric("Blues", domain = sf_Apsy_wgs84$weight_foraging, na.color = "transparent")
pal_res <- colorNumeric("Reds", domain = log10(sf_Apsy_wgs84$resistance), na.color = "transparent")

# Mapping strict pour Leaflet basé sur ref_ocsge
pal_ocsge <- colorFactor(palette = ref_ocsge$couleur, levels = ref_ocsge$nomenclature)

leaflet(sf_Apsy_wgs84) %>%
  addProviderTiles(providers$CartoDB.Positron) %>%

  # Layer: OCS-GE
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal_ocsge(nomenclature), color = "white", weight = 0.5, fillOpacity = 0.7,
    group = "OCS-GE", label = ~paste(nomenclature)
  ) %>%

  # Layer: Suitability
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal_wg(suitability), color = NA, fillOpacity = 0.7,
    group = "Suitability", label = ~paste("Suitability:", suitability)
  ) %>%

  # Layer: Foraging
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal_wf(weight_foraging), color = NA, fillOpacity = 0.7,
    group = "Foraging Weight", label = ~paste("Foraging:", weight_foraging)
  ) %>%

  # Layer: Resistance
  addPolygons(
    fillColor = ~pal_res(log10(resistance)), color = NA, fillOpacity = 0.7,
    group = "Resistance", label = ~paste("Resistance:", resistance)
  ) %>%

  # Controls
  addLayersControl(
    baseGroups = c("OCS-GE", "Suitability", "Foraging Weight", "Resistance"),
    options = layersControlOptions(collapsed = FALSE)
  ) %>%
  addLegend(pal = pal_ocsge, values = ref_ocsge$nomenclature, title = "OCS-GE", group = "OCS-GE", position = "bottomright")
```

# Connectivity

## From habitat to raster of source and resistance

1. first step is to collect habitat of the OCS-GE as we did previously

```{r plt_apsy}
apsy_hab <- join_ocsge_species(sf_ocsge, "Apodemus_sylvaticus")
plot_species_habitat(apsy_hab)
```

2. then, we have to create an `habitat` object to benefit from `spacemodR` functionalities

```{r habitat_apsy}
apsy_habitat <- habitat(apsy_hab, habitat=TRUE, weight=apsy_hab$suitability, touches=FALSE)
apsy_resistance <- habitat(apsy_hab, habitat=TRUE, weight=apsy_hab$resistance, touches=FALSE)
```

Here `touches = FALSE` gives each pixel to the land cover class lying under its centre,
which is the right rule for a map of contiguous polygons. The role of this argument,
and of `priority`, is detailed [below](#stacking-order-and-thin-structures-priority-and-touches).


3. converting them in raster

```{r, echo=FALSE}
rast_Apsy_habitat <- load_raster_repo("rast_Apsy_habitat.tif")
rast_Apsy_resistance <- load_raster_repo("rast_Apsy_resistance.tif")
```

```{r}
ground_cd <- load_raster_extdata("ground_concentration_cd_compressed.tif")
```


```{r plt_apsy_habitat, eval=FALSE}
rast_Apsy_habitat <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, apsy_habitat)
```

The `resistance` of `ocsge_species_dict` is already on the exponential scale
that connectivity models expect, from 1 (free movement) to 100 (impassable): it
is derived from the `permeability` score in $[0-10]$ as
`10^(2 * (1 - permeability / 10))`. A resistance must be at least 1, so the
pixels lying outside the land cover map, which `habitat_raster()` leaves at 0,
are set to 1.

```{r plt_apsy_resistance}
rast_Apsy_resistance <- habitat_raster(ground_cd, apsy_resistance)
rast_Apsy_resistance <- ifel(rast_Apsy_resistance < 1, 1, rast_Apsy_resistance)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# terra::writeRaster(rast_Apsy_habitat, "inst/extdata/rast_Apsy_habitat.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
# terra::writeRaster(rast_Apsy_resistance, "inst/extdata/rast_Apsy_resistance.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
```

```{r}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(rast_Apsy_habitat, main = "Suitability")
plot(log10(rast_Apsy_resistance), main = "Resistance (log10)")
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```


```{r, eval=FALSE}
terra::writeRaster(rast_Apsy_habitat, "julia_run/rast_Apsy_habitat.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
terra::writeRaster(rast_Apsy_resistance, "julia_run/rast_Apsy_resistance.tif", overwrite = TRUE)
```


## Stacking order and thin structures: `priority` and `touches`

A raster holds a single value per pixel, while several features of the `habitat`
object often share the same pixel. Two settings, given layer by layer in
`add_habitat()` and `add_nohabitat()`, decide what the pixel gets:

* `priority` answers *"which layer wins where layers overlap?"*. The layers are
  stacked from the lowest to the highest priority and the pixel takes the value
  of the layer on top. By default each new layer goes on top of the previous
  ones, so the layers stack in the order they are added.
* `touches` answers *"which pixels does a feature occupy?"*. With `touches = TRUE`
  (the default) a line or a polygon fills every pixel it touches. With
  `touches = FALSE` a polygon only fills the pixels whose centre it covers, and
  a line only the pixels of a thin line.

Neither of them describes how hard a structure is to cross: this is the role of
the `weight` (a resistance), or of `add_nohabitat()` for an absolute barrier.
A river is a barrier for the wood mouse and hardly an obstacle for a flying
insect: this is written in the weights of two different `habitat` objects, not
in `touches`.

### Example: a watercourse in the landscape of *Apodemus sylvaticus*

Let us zoom on a window of 1 km x 1 km where a channel, narrower than a pixel
(about 25 m), joins a larger canal. Water surfaces are not a habitat for the wood
mouse: we take them out of the land cover and declare them with `add_nohabitat()`.

```{r win_data}
win <- st_as_sfc(st_bbox(
  c(xmin = 700100, xmax = 701100, ymin = 7036400, ymax = 7037400),
  crs = st_crs(apsy_hab)
))
apsy_win <- st_intersection(apsy_hab, win)
grid_win <- crop(ground_cd, vect(win))

water_win <- apsy_win[apsy_win$code_cs == "CS1.2.2", ]
land_win <- apsy_win[apsy_win$code_cs != "CS1.2.2", ]
```

We build the same landscape with three different rules:

```{r win_habitat}
# 1. everything by pixel centre
hab_centre <- habitat() |>
  add_habitat(land_win, weight = land_win$resistance, touches = FALSE) |>
  add_nohabitat(water_win, touches = FALSE)

# 2. water on every touched pixel, but below the land cover
hab_below <- habitat() |>
  add_habitat(land_win, weight = land_win$resistance, touches = FALSE, priority = 2) |>
  add_nohabitat(water_win, touches = TRUE, priority = 1)

# 3. water on every touched pixel, on top of the land cover
hab_top <- habitat() |>
  add_habitat(land_win, weight = land_win$resistance, touches = FALSE, priority = 1) |>
  add_nohabitat(water_win, touches = TRUE, priority = 2)

rast_win <- list(
  "1. pixel centre" = habitat_raster(grid_win, hab_centre),
  "2. touches, water below" = habitat_raster(grid_win, hab_below),
  "3. touches, water on top" = habitat_raster(grid_win, hab_top)
)
```

In the maps below, the excluded pixels (`NA`) are in dark grey and the outline of
the water polygons is drawn in blue.

```{r plt_win, echo=FALSE, fig.height=4}
plot_win <- function(r, title) {
  ggplot() +
    theme_minimal() +
    geom_spatraster(data = r) +
    geom_sf(data = water_win, fill = NA, color = "#2b8cbe", linewidth = 0.3) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#fff5f0", high = "#67000d", limits = c(0, 10),
                        na.value = "grey20", name = "Resistance") +
    labs(title = title) +
    theme(axis.text = element_blank())
}
wrap_plots(Map(plot_win, rast_win, names(rast_win)), guides = "collect")
```

To compare them, we count the excluded pixels, the number of separate pieces
the watercourse is made of, and the number of patches of land a mouse can reach
without crossing water (pixels being neighbours by their edges and their
corners):

```{r win_table}
data.frame(
  rule = names(rast_win),
  water_pixels = sapply(rast_win, function(r) sum(is.na(values(r)))),
  water_pieces = sapply(rast_win, function(r) {
    nrow(unique(patches(ifel(is.na(r), 1, NA), directions = 8)))
  }),
  land_patches = sapply(rast_win, function(r) {
    nrow(unique(patches(r, directions = 8)))
  }),
  row.names = NULL
)
```

1. **Pixel centre.** The channel only keeps the few pixels whose centre falls
   in it: it is cut into separate pieces, and even the larger canal can be
   crossed diagonally between two of its pixels. The land is a single patch:
   for the model, the water is not a barrier.
2. **Touches, water below.** The water is drawn on every pixel it touches, but
   the land cover is stacked on top of it and takes back all the pixels whose
   centre it covers. `touches` alone is not enough.
3. **Touches, water on top.** The watercourse is in one piece and the canal
   splits the land in two patches. This is the combination to use for a
   structure that must stay continuous: `touches = TRUE` **and** a `priority`
   above the layers it runs through.

### Choosing `touches`

`touches = TRUE` has a price: the feature is drawn larger than it is. In the
example the water covers about 4.2 ha, that is 67 pixels: the pixel-centre rule
gives 66 pixels, the third rule 144.

* Use `touches = FALSE` for layers of contiguous polygons covering the landscape
  (a land cover map such as OCS-GE). Their surfaces stay unbiased, and with
  `touches = TRUE` each class would spread over the border pixels of its
  neighbours.
* Keep `touches = TRUE` for the thin structures whose continuity matters:
  barriers (rivers, roads, fences) and corridors (hedgerows, banks), whether
  they are drawn as lines or as narrow polygons, and give them a higher
  `priority`.
* It also applies to structures that are only partly permeable. A river added
  with `add_habitat()` and a high resistance must be continuous as well,
  otherwise it is crossed for free wherever it runs obliquely to the grid.

Some situations have no good answer at a given resolution: a structure narrower
than a pixel is either widened to a full pixel or lost, a gap smaller than a
pixel (a bridge) disappears unless it is added as its own layer with a higher
priority, and two structures sharing a pixel (a hedgerow along a road) cannot
both be kept, `priority` only choosing the winner. When these cases matter, the
solution is a finer `ground_raster`.

## Omniscape

4. defining a radius

To define the radius, we have to know the real distance radius and then convert it into number of pixel.
Let say, we have a dispersal radius of 500m for *Apodemus sylvaticus*,
which is actually quite large for that species.

Here the map has pixels of 24m, so we use this large value for examples.

For pixel, the size is given by `res(raster)`, here it is a meter system:
 
```{r}
# get pixel size
terra::res(ground_cd)
# convert meter radius to pixel radius
m_radius = 500
px_radius = 500 / res(ground_cd)[1]
px_radius
```

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
docker run --rm \
  -v "$(pwd)/julia_run:/julia_run" \
  spacemodr Rscript /julia_run/run_dispersal.R \
  /julia_run/rast_Apsy_habitat.tif \
  /julia_run/rast_Apsy_resistance.tif \
  20.05 \
  omniscape_apsy_500m
```

```{bash, eval=FALSE}
docker run --rm \
  -v "$(pwd)/julia_run:/julia_run" \
  spacemodr Rscript /julia_run/run_dispersal.R \
  /julia_run/rast_Apsy_habitat.tif \
  /julia_run/rast_Apsy_resistance.tif \
  8.02 \
  omniscape_apsy_200m
```

```{r load_omniscape, echo=FALSE}
omniscape_apsy_200m <- load_raster_repo("omniscape_apsy_200m.tif")
omniscape_apsy_500m <- load_raster_repo("omniscape_apsy_500m.tif")
```


```{r plt_omniscape}
p_src = ggplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_spatraster(data = rast_Apsy_habitat) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#ffffe5", high = "#004529", na.value = "transparent", name = "Suitability") +
  labs(title = "Source")

p_res = ggplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_spatraster(data = rast_Apsy_resistance) +
  scale_fill_gradient(
    low = "#fff5f0", high = "#67000d", transform="log10",
    na.value = "transparent", name = "Resistance")+
  labs(title = "Resistance")

max_r200m <- global(omniscape_apsy_200m, fun = "max", na.rm = TRUE)
norm_r200m <- omniscape_apsy_200m / as.numeric(max_r200m)
p_omn_200m = ggplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_spatraster(data = norm_r200m) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("white", "#11dddd", "#dddd11", "red"),
    trans = "sqrt", 
    na.value = "transparent") +
  labs(title = "Omniscape Connectivity (r=200m)", fill = "Probability")

max_r500m <- global(omniscape_apsy_500m, fun = "max", na.rm = TRUE)
norm_r500m <- omniscape_apsy_500m / as.numeric(max_r500m)
p_omn_500m = ggplot() +
  theme_minimal() +
  geom_spatraster(data = norm_r500m) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(
    colours = c("white", "#11dddd", "#dddd11", "red"),
    trans = "sqrt", na.value = "transparent") +
  labs(title = "Omniscape Connectivity (r=500m)", fill = "Probability")

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_src, p_res, p_omn_200m, p_omn_500m, ncol=2)
```
